title: Query Processing & Optimization
summary: SQL is declarative — you say what you want, not how. The optimizer's job is to find the fastest plan. Learn the pipeline, cost model, and join algorithms that make it work.

blocks.markdown:
When you run a SQL query, the database does far more than just look up rows.

- It **parses** the SQL, **translates** to a logical plan, then **optimizes** before ever touching data.
- Most cost comes from **disk I/O** — reading pages from storage.
- The optimizer picks among many equivalent plans to minimize that cost.
- Understanding this lets you write faster queries and read EXPLAIN output.

A query travels through four stages before you see results.

<<< Image: left-to-right horizontal pipeline diagram, 4 boxes connected by arrows, clean blue/grey palette. Box 1: 'SQL Text → Parser (syntax check)'. Box 2: 'Parse Tree → Translator (relational algebra)'. Box 3: 'Logical Plan → Optimizer (picks best physical plan)'. Box 4: 'Physical Plan → Execution Engine → Result'. Label above: Query Processing Pipeline. >>>

- **Parse** — check syntax, produce a parse tree.
- **Translate** — rewrite as relational algebra (select, project, join operators).
- **Optimize** — explore plan alternatives, estimate costs, pick cheapest.
- **Execute** — run the physical plan, return rows.

The optimizer assigns a **cost** to each plan and picks the lowest.

- Cost is measured mostly in **disk I/O** — the number of disk pages read or written. CPU is cheap compared to I/O.
- A **page** (or block) is the unit of disk transfer, typically 8 KB. Fetching one page from disk takes ~10 ms — millions of times slower than RAM.
- Secondary: CPU cycles, network (in distributed DBs).

See [storage-file-organization](storage-file-organization) for how pages are laid out.

blocks.subTitle: External merge sort
blocks.markdown:
**External merge sort** is how databases sort data bigger than RAM — used inside sort-merge join and ORDER BY.

**Two phases:**
- **Sort phase** — load as many pages as fit in RAM, sort them in-memory, write a **run** (sorted chunk) to disk. Repeat until all data is in runs.
- **Merge phase** — repeatedly merge pairs of runs (reading one page per run at a time) until one sorted file remains.

Cost ≈ 2 × N × (1 + ⌈log runs⌉) page I/Os, where N = total pages.

blocks.subTitle: Nested-loop join
blocks.markdown:
**Nested-loop join (NLJ)** is the simplest join: for every row in the outer table, scan every row in the inner table and emit matching pairs.

- Cost: |outer| × |inner| page reads — **quadratic**.
- Works for any join condition, including inequalities.
- Only practical when one table is tiny (fits in a page or two).

blocks.subTitle: Block nested-loop & index nested-loop
blocks.markdown:
Two improvements over basic NLJ:

- **Block nested-loop (BNLJ)** — load a **block** of outer rows into RAM at once, then scan the inner table once per block. Cost drops to ⌈|outer pages| / buffer size⌉ × |inner pages|.
- **Index nested-loop (INLJ)** — instead of scanning the inner table, use an [indexing](indexing) on the join column to look up only matching rows. Cost ≈ |outer| × index-lookup cost. Best when the inner table has a suitable index.

blocks.subTitle: Sort-merge join
blocks.markdown:
**Sort-merge join (SMJ)** sorts both tables on the join key, then merges them in one linear pass.

- After sorting, each table is read once → **O(N + M)** for the merge.
- Dominates when both inputs are already sorted (e.g. from an index scan or a prior sort).
- Also handles non-equality joins like `A.x < B.y`.
- Expensive sorting cost amortized if the sorted order is reused later.

blocks.subTitle: Hash join
blocks.markdown:
**Hash join** builds an in-memory hash table on the smaller table, then probes it for every row in the larger table.

- Probe phase is one pass per table → **O(N + M)** like sort-merge, but no sorting needed.
- Requires the hash table (smaller table) to **fit in RAM**. Spills to disk if it doesn't.
- Only works for **equality joins** (`A.id = B.id`).
- Usually the fastest join for large tables without useful indexes.

blocks.subTitle: When each join wins
blocks.markdown:
Choose based on data size, indexes, and join type.

| Algorithm | Best when |
|---|---|
| Index nested-loop | Inner table has index on join key |
| Hash join | Large tables, equality join, enough RAM |
| Sort-merge join | Inputs already sorted, or inequality join |

- Nested-loop (basic) rarely wins at scale — only if outer table is one page.
- Optimizers pick automatically; understanding this helps you add the right index.

Query plans are trees of operators. Intermediate results can flow in two ways:

- **Materialization** — each operator writes its full result to a temp table on disk before the next operator starts. Simple, but expensive in I/O.
- **Pipelining** — operators run concurrently; rows pass from parent to child one at a time through a buffer, never fully landing on disk.

Pipelining is preferred — it saves disk writes. Materialization is forced when an operator needs to see all input before producing any output (e.g., sort, hash build phase).

**Heuristic (rule-based) optimization** transforms a logical plan using rules that almost always help, without computing costs.

Key rules:
- **Push selections down** — apply filters as early as possible to reduce row count before joins.
- **Push projections down** — drop unneeded columns early to shrink row width.
- **Reorder joins** — put the join that produces fewest rows first.

Fast and cheap, but can miss a better plan when statistics would reveal a different order.

**Cost-based optimization (CBO)** enumerates multiple plan alternatives, estimates the cost of each using statistics, and picks the cheapest.

- **Statistics** stored per column: number of distinct values, min/max, and a **histogram** (a bucketed count of how often each value range appears).
- **Selectivity** = fraction of rows a predicate keeps. Low selectivity = few rows pass = filter is very effective.
- Optimizer uses selectivity to estimate intermediate result sizes, then cost each join order.
- Stats can go stale — `ANALYZE` (Postgres) or `UPDATE STATISTICS` (SQL Server) refreshes them.

EXPLAIN shows the **query plan** the optimizer chose — the tree of operators and estimated costs.

```
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id WHERE u.country = 'IN';

Hash Join  (cost=120..980 rows=4200) (actual rows=4187)
  Hash Cond: (o.user_id = u.id)
  -> Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0..540 rows=42000)
  -> Hash  (cost=60..60 rows=480)
       -> Index Scan on users  (cost=0..60 rows=480)
            Filter: (country = 'IN')
```

- **Seq Scan** — full table scan (no useful index).
- **Index Scan** — used an index; filtered to 480 rows before the join.
- **Hash Join** — built hash on users (smaller), probed with orders.
- `cost=start..total` — estimated I/O units; `rows` — estimated output.
- **ANALYZE** runs the query and shows *actual* rows vs estimated — gaps indicate stale stats.

See [advanced-sql](advanced-sql) for EXPLAIN usage patterns.

Common optimizer traps:

- **Stale statistics** — if you bulk-load data without running ANALYZE, the optimizer uses wrong row counts and picks a bad plan.
- **Over-indexing** — too many indexes means more choices, slower writes, and the optimizer can pick a bad index scan over a faster seq scan for large result sets.
- **Functions on indexed columns** — `WHERE UPPER(email) = 'X'` prevents index use; use a functional index instead.
- **Forcing a plan** — hints (`/*+ INDEX(t idx) */`) lock in a plan that may become wrong as data changes.

blocks.subTitle: How the optimizer picks a plan
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How does a query optimizer choose which plan to execute?**

It enumerates plan alternatives (different join orders, access methods), estimates the cost of each using statistics — row counts, histograms, selectivity — and picks the plan with lowest estimated I/O. Heuristics (push filters down) are applied first to prune the search space; then cost-based selection picks among the survivors.

blocks.subTitle: Hash join vs sort-merge join
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: When would you use hash join vs sort-merge join?**

**Hash join** wins when tables are large, inputs are unsorted, the join is an equality, and the smaller table fits in RAM. **Sort-merge** wins when inputs are already sorted (e.g., from indexes), when the join is an inequality (`<`, `>`), or when the sorted output is reused downstream. Both are O(N+M) for the join phase; hash join avoids the sort cost.

blocks.subTitle: Heuristic vs cost-based
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the difference between heuristic and cost-based optimization?**

**Heuristic** applies fixed rules (push selections down, reorder joins) without looking at data. Fast, always safe, but can miss optimal plans. **Cost-based** uses real statistics to estimate I/O and compare plans numerically — finds better plans but depends on stats being fresh. Modern optimizers do both: heuristics first to shrink the search space, then cost-based to pick the winner.
